opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think fundamentally science has always been a global endeavor. Some of the greatest advances in history came from people crossing borders, sharing ideas, and building on each other's work. When you have students and researchers moving in both directions, studying in each other's universities, working in each other's labs, you build an understanding at a human level that's very hard to get any other way. You realize that the people on the other side are, by and large, motivated by the same things you are: curiosity, wanting to solve hard problems, wanting to do something good for the world.

And that matters enormously right now, especially with something as consequential as AI. We're heading toward technologies that will affect everyone on the planet, and at some point we're going to need international cooperation on things like safety standards and how these systems get deployed. That kind of cooperation is so much easier if there's already a foundation of trust and personal relationships between the scientific communities. If everything becomes siloed and adversarial, with no exchange at all, you lose those channels just when you might need them most.

Of course, you have to be thoughtful. There are legitimate security concerns and you can't be naive about them. But I think the default should be openness and exchange, especially in fundamental science. The more we understand each other, the less likely we are to fall into a pure race dynamic where everyone cuts corners. Ultimately I'd like to see something more like a CERN-style collaborative effort for the final steps toward AGI, and that's only possible if we keep those bridges open now.

r001.rationale: The response says that students and researchers moving between countries builds human-level understanding and helps people recognize shared motivations, presenting this as a reason to favor cross-border movement.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's one of the most powerful things we have, honestly. If you look at the history of science, the big leaps almost always came from the mixing of ideas and cultures. People moving around, studying in different places, carrying ideas back with them. That's how knowledge has always propagated, and I don't think AI is any different.

So at a practical level, you have incredibly talented people on both sides. Some of the best researchers I've worked with over the years came through that route, studying in the UK or the US and then either staying or going back. And when they go back, they carry with them not just technical knowledge but a set of norms, ways of thinking about safety, about scientific openness, about how you do rigorous research. That's not a small thing. That's how a shared culture of science actually develops.

And then on the bigger picture, I've said for a long time that I think AI is going to be one of the most consequential technologies humanity ever builds, and it has to be done in a way where there's some global coordination on safety. You can't really get there if the two most capable scientific communities in the world don't know each other, don't trust each other, have never sat in the same lab or the same conference. The people-to-people connections are the thing that make the harder conversations possible later. If you've spent years working alongside someone, you can pick up the phone.

I'm not naive about it. There are legitimate national security concerns, and there are things that governments have to think carefully about, and I understand that. But I'd be very worried if the answer became to shut things down entirely, to decouple completely. I think that makes the world less safe, not more. Science has always been one of the great bridges between nations, even at the height of the Cold War you had physicists talking to each other, and I'd like to think AI could play that role too rather than becoming purely a race. So on balance I come down firmly on the side of keeping those doors open, with sensible guardrails, because I think the long-term benefits for everyone are enormous.

r001.rationale: The response says people moving between the West and China mix ideas and cultures, spread knowledge, and build shared scientific culture and trust—human benefits it gives as reasons to keep migration and education channels open.

astra-6.text:
I think the exchange of people and ideas is incredibly valuable. When you study or work in another country, you build friendships and understand how people there think. You see them as individuals, and that can help break down some of the suspicion that develops between countries.

In science, especially, progress depends on sharing knowledge and bringing different perspectives together. I’d like that exchange to go both ways, with people from China studying and working in the West, and Western students and researchers spending time in China. Of course, there are security concerns that need to be taken seriously. But we also need those human connections if we’re going to cooperate on problems that affect everyone, including making AI safe.

r001.rationale: The response says cross-country study and work build friendships, help people understand one another as individuals, and reduce suspicion, and explicitly favors exchange in both directions.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s important that people have opportunities to understand one another. When you study or work in another country, you build friendships and discover how much you have in common. That’s much harder to get from a distance.

And I think that exchange should go both ways. We want talented people coming here, but there’s also value in people from the West going to China and understanding it better. It doesn’t mean ignoring disagreements or security concerns. It means keeping human connections strong enough that we can talk about those differences and cooperate on problems that affect everybody.

r001.rationale: The response favors two-way exchange between the West and China because studying or working abroad builds friendships and helps people understand one another and their commonalities.
